name: Nepal
summary_text: Nepal is workable for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since the landmark 2007 Sunil Babu Pant decision; a third-gender “O” category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled (Rukshana Kapali case) that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu has an established activist scene (Blue Diamond Society, founded 2001). The gap between doctrine and practice is large: HRW documents (“We Have to Beg So Many People,” 2024) that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces like Madhesh face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet. For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside Kathmandu/Pokhara bubbles.

sources.title: Nepal: Barriers to Transgender Legal Recognition | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch (Feb 2024): 'Nepal: Barriers to Transgender Legal Recognition' — despite progressive court rulings, documentary recognition remains bogged in medical and bureaucratic barriers.

sources.title: Nepal Supreme Court grants legal recognition to transgender woman without medical verification - JURIST - News
sources.claim_summary: JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali should be legally recognised on all documents as a woman without medical verification - after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021. Context: 'other'/third-gender categories exist since a 2007 ruling, but changing markers to male/female usually requires surgery abroad plus intrusive post-operative genital exams.

sources.title: Nepal’s Trans Rights Reputation Needs to be Matched With Real Policy – The Diplomat
sources.claim_summary: The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's trans-rights reputation needs to be matched with real policy - the country's LGBTIQ+ rights record is more complicated than it first appears; progressive reputation vs implementation gaps.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024): the complexity of transgender life in Janakpur - nine trans people sharing a flat; discrimination in public spaces and government institutions, physical and sexual harassment; celebrated as entertainers but objectified and ridiculed.

APTN (Asia Pacific Transgender Network) publication (Oct 2021, in Nepali): 'Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078: Civil Society Proposal' - by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi, produced through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship; a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition in Nepal.

The Record (Sept 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: 'The reality of transgender rights in Nepal' - challenges the 'beacon for LGBT rights' narrative; the dominant claim that the Constitution allows self-determined gender markers (from Sunil Babu Pant v Government of Nepal, 2007) masks 'numerous bureaucratic and administrative hurdles and the lack of inclusive legislative measures'; uses the activist-coined term PoMSOGIESC.

SIT Study Abroad ISP (Spring 2015) by Sophia Greene: 'Gender and Sexuality in Nepal: The Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minorities in a Rapidly Changing Social Climate' - despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.
